title: First-principles carrier mobility and optical absorption of strained ZnO with self-consistent Hubbard interactions
summary: Carrier mobility and optical absorption are key performance parameters of oxide semiconductors in transparent and flexible displays. We use a newly developed density-functional perturbation theory with a self-consistent Hubbard correction (DFPT+U) to study phonon-limited electron transport and phonon-assisted optical absorption in strained zinc oxide (ZnO). This parameter-free approach accounts for electron-phonon interactions and on-site correlation effects simultaneously. Electronic structures and phonon dispersions are computed under three distinct uniaxial strain directions. Uniaxial tensile strain up to 4.8% along [\bar110] is found to increase the room-temperature electron mobility by 19% while leaving visible-range optical absorption essentially unchanged. These results demonstrate that moderate strain can selectively enhance carrier transport without degrading optical transparency, and establish DFPT+U as an effective framework for predicting strain-dependent transport and optical properties in wide-band-gap oxides with implications for strain-engineered display and optoelectronic applications.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a parameter-free method (DFPT+U) to simultaneously study electron-phonon interactions and on-site correlation effects in strained zinc oxide, finding that moderate tensile strain can enhance carrier mobility by 19% without compromising optical transparency.
AI.motivation: To address the need for high-performance oxide semiconductors in transparent and flexible displays by understanding how strain affects carrier mobility and optical absorption properties.
AI.method: A newly developed density-functional perturbation theory with self-consistent Hubbard correction (DFPT+U) was used to compute electronic structures, phonon dispersions, phonon-limited electron transport, and phonon-assisted optical absorption under three uniaxial strain directions.
AI.result: Uniaxial tensile strain up to 4.8% along [\bar110] direction increases room-temperature electron mobility by 19% while leaving visible-range optical absorption essentially unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Moderate strain can selectively enhance carrier transport without degrading optical transparency, and DFPT+U is an effective framework for predicting strain-dependent transport and optical properties in wide-band-gap oxides for strain-engineered display and optoelectronic applications.

title: Magnetic properties of a quasi-two-dimensional spin-1/2 antiferromagnet Y2CuGe4O12
summary: Competing magnetic interactions and frustration-induced quantum fluctuations in spatially anisotropic low-dimensional magnets often give rise to exotic magnetic phenomena, including field-induced phases. Here, we present crystal structure, magnetic susceptibility, specific heat, and electron spin resonance (ESR) measurements on polycrystalline Y$2$CuGe$4$O${12}$, supported by density functional theory (DFT) calculations. In this compound, the Cu$^{2+}$ ions form a distorted triangular lattice with competing intraplanar ferromagnetic ($J_1 \approx 0.138$ K and $J_2 \approx 0.01$ K) and antiferromagnetic ($J_3 \approx -3.22$ K) exchange interactions, together with a weaker interplanar antiferromagnetic coupling ($J_4 \approx -1.56$ K). These interactions account for the small Curie--Weiss temperature, $θ{\rm CW}=-1.8$ K. Despite the dominant antiferromagnetic interactions, no signature of long-range magnetic ordering is observed down to 0.4 K. Instead, broad maxima in both the magnetic susceptibility and magnetic specific heat reveal the development of short-range spin correlations, further supported by the critical ESR linewidth broadening characteristic of low-dimensional frustrated magnets. Application of an external magnetic field progressively suppresses the broad maximum in the magnetic specific heat, reflecting competition between the Zeeman and exchange energy scales, and drives the system into a field-polarized state above the saturation field, $μ_0H_{\rm s}=2.6$ T. In this regime, the magnetic specific heat exhibits an exponential temperature dependence, consistent with gapped magnon excitations. These results establish Y$_2$CuGe$4$O${12}$ as a rare distorted triangular-lattice magnet in which further-neighbor exchange interactions dominate the magnetic behavior, providing a promising platform for exploring frustration-driven quantum phenomena.

AI.tldr: Y2CuGe4O12 is a distorted triangular-lattice magnet where competing ferromagnetic (J1≈0.138 K, J2≈0.01 K) and dominant antiferromagnetic (J3≈-3.22 K) interactions, combined with interplanar coupling (J4≈-1.56 K), lead to quantum frustration. Despite dominant AFM interactions, no long-range ordering occurs down to 0.4 K; instead, short-range spin correlations develop. Application of external magnetic field (μ0Hs=2.6 T) drives the system into a field-polarized state with gapped magnon excitations.
AI.motivation: Explore field-induced phases and quantum phenomena in spatially anisotropic low-dimensional magnets with competing magnetic interactions and frustration-induced quantum fluctuations. The study aims to find rare distorted triangular-lattice magnets where further-neighbor exchange interactions dominate magnetic behavior.
AI.method: Combined experimental techniques (magnetic susceptibility, specific heat, ESR measurements) on polycrystalline Y2CuGe4O12, supported by density functional theory (DFT) calculations to determine exchange parameters.
AI.result: Identified competing intraplanar FM (J1, J2) and AFM (J3) interactions plus weaker interplanar AFM coupling (J4). No long-range ordering observed down to 0.4 K; broad maxima in susceptibility and specific heat indicate short-range spin correlations. ESR shows critical linewidth broadening. External magnetic field suppresses the broad maximum and drives system into field-polarized state above μ0Hs=2.6 T, where magnetic specific heat shows exponential temperature dependence (gapped magnons).
AI.conclusion: Y2CuGe4O12 represents a rare distorted triangular-lattice magnet where further-neighbor exchange interactions dominate, providing a promising platform for exploring frustration-driven quantum phenomena without long-range ordering.

title: Charge-Density-Wave Phase Selection by Janus-Induced Intrinsic Strain in Monolayer NbSSiAs$_2$
summary: Controlling phase selection among competing charge-density-wave (CDW) instabilities remains challenging in two-dimensional materials. Here, first-principles calculations show that Janus-induced intrinsic tensile strain redirects the off-M soft-mode tendency of NbS$_2$ to the M point in NbSSiAs$_2$, selecting a $2\times2$ CDW reconstruction. Electron-phonon coupling analysis identifies momentum-selective coupling between Nb-derived states and a longitudinal acoustic mode as the origin of the M-point instability. The reconstructed phase hosts two nearly degenerate Nb-trimerized configurations whose relative stability is tuned by biaxial strain. Both configurations retain phonon-mediated superconductivity on the 6-7 K scale, indicating the coexistence of CDW order and superconductivity. Compressive strain favors the 1+3-hollow configuration and induces a band-inverted, $Z_2$-nontrivial state while preserving superconductivity. Together, these results identify Janus-induced intrinsic strain as an internal structural route for CDW phase selection, whereas external strain provides access to a regime in which CDW order, topology, and superconductivity coexist.

AI.tldr: Janus-induced intrinsic tensile strain in NbSSiAs2 redirects charge-density-wave (CDW) instabilities from the off-M to M point, selecting a 2×2 CDW reconstruction. The reconstructed phase hosts two nearly degenerate Nb-trimerized configurations tunable by biaxial strain, with both retaining superconductivity at 6-7 K. Compressive strain induces a band-inverted Z2-nontrivial state while preserving superconductivity, demonstrating coexistence of CDW order, topology, and superconductivity.
AI.motivation: Controlling phase selection among competing charge-density-wave instabilities remains challenging in two-dimensional materials. The researchers sought to identify an internal structural route for CDW phase selection using Janus-induced intrinsic strain.
AI.method: First-principles calculations and electron-phonon coupling analysis were employed to investigate the CDW instabilities in NbS2 and NbSSiAs2. Momentum-selective coupling between Nb-derived states and a longitudinal acoustic mode was identified as the origin of the M-point instability.
AI.result: Janus-induced intrinsic tensile strain redirects the off-M soft-mode tendency of NbS2 to the M point in NbSSiAs2, selecting a 2×2 CDW reconstruction. Two nearly degenerate Nb-trimerized configurations (1+3-hollow and 3+1-hill) were identified, with relative stability tunable by biaxial strain. Both configurations retain phonon-mediated superconductivity on the 6-7 K scale. Compressive strain favors the 1+3-hollow configuration and induces a band-inverted, Z2-nontrivial topological state while preserving superconductivity.
AI.conclusion: Janus-induced intrinsic strain serves as an internal structural route for CDW phase selection in 2D materials, while external strain provides access to a regime where CDW order, topology, and superconductivity coexist. This work establishes a strategy for engineering multifunctional electronic states through strain engineering.

title: Domain-Selective Enhancement of Second Harmonic Generation in Monolayer MoS$_2$ via Ferroelectricity-Controlled Photodoping
summary: Hybrid heterostructures combining two-dimensional semiconductors with ferroelectric materials offer a versatile route to actively control light-matter interactions at the nanoscale. Here, we report all-optical, light-induced domain-selective control of second-harmonic generation (SHG) in monolayer molybdenum disulfide (MoS$_2$) integrated with periodically poled lithium niobate (LiNbO$_3$). Spatially resolved SHG imaging reveals a pronounced modulation of the nonlinear optical response of monolayer MoS$_2$ governed by the ferroelectric domain pattern of the underlying substrate. A strong SHG contrast is observed between domains of opposite polarization, with a marked dependence on both the excitation wavelength and the incident optical power. The comparison between ferroelectric domains that either enable or do not exhibit light-driven photodoping in the MoS$_2$ monolayer provides a direct assessment of the role of carrier density in the nonlinear optical response. We find that ferroelectric-polarization-controlled photodoping at the MoS$_2$/LiNbO$_3$ interface enhances the effective second-order susceptibility, $χ^2$, producing an increase in SHG intensity of up to ~70% under resonant excitation conditions. Ab initio calculations corroborate that charge doping modifies the electronic band structure of MoS$_2$ and strongly affects $χ^2$ in the resonant regime, providing microscopic support for the experimentally observed modulation. The results highlight the combination of light intensity and ferroelectricity as a powerful knob for band-structure modulation in 2D materials and reconfigurable nonlinear optical responses, opening pathways toward programmable frequency conversion, smart light modulators, and advanced nonlinear photonic functionalities in integrated hybrid platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates all-optical control of second-harmonic generation (SHG) in monolayer MoS2 integrated with periodically poled lithium niobate (LiNbO3) by leveraging ferroelectric domain patterns and light-induced photodoping effects.
AI.motivation: The research aims to actively control light-matter interactions at the nanoscale in hybrid 2D semiconductor/ferroelectric platforms, motivated by the need for programmable frequency conversion and reconfigurable nonlinear optical devices.
AI.method: The study combines spatially resolved SHG imaging to map the nonlinear optical response across ferroelectric domains, along with ab initio calculations to understand the microscopic mechanisms. The wavelength and power dependence of SHG contrast was systematically investigated.
AI.result: A strong SHG contrast between domains of opposite polarization was observed, with up to ~70% increase in SHG intensity under resonant excitation. Ferroelectric-polarization-controlled photodoping at the MoS2/LiNbO3 interface was identified as the key mechanism enhancing the effective second-order susceptibility χ².
AI.conclusion: The combination of light intensity and ferroelectricity provides a powerful approach for band-structure modulation in 2D materials, enabling reconfigurable nonlinear optical responses. This opens pathways toward programmable frequency conversion, smart light modulators, and advanced nonlinear photonic functionalities in integrated hybrid platforms.

title: Strength-degradation phase-field regularization of cohesive fracture: the antiplane case
comment: 43 pages, 18 figures, 1 table. Submitted to Comptes Rendus. Mecanique
summary: Phase-field approaches to fracture, initially designed as regularization of the Griffith model of brittle fracture, are now commonly viewed as gradient-damage models whose regularization length becomes a material property driving crack nucleation. One weakness of this approach is that the strength surface cannot be arbitrary: its shape is dictated by the elastic energy, and its magnitude by the regularization length. We focus on the antiplane version of the model introduced by Bourdin, Marigo, Maurini and Zolesi (arXiv:2506.22558), which handles crack propagation along unknown paths and nucleation governed by an arbitrary convex strength surface by degrading the strength instead of the stiffness. It can be interpreted as a regularization of softening plasticity in which localization bands obey an equivalent cohesive law set by the strength domain and the toughness, while the role of the regularization length, when small compared to the elasto-cohesive length, is purely numerical. Strength, stiffness, and toughness thus become independent material data, and limit analysis, perfect plasticity, cohesive fracture, and brittle fracture merge into a single variational framework. We derive closed-form solutions for a simple shear problem, propose a numerical scheme combining alternate minimization and conic programming, and numerically verify the equivalent cohesive law, its independence of the regularization, and the size effect governed by the elasto-cohesive length. A "surfing" simulation highlights the structure of the propagating crack while a re-entrant V-notch is used to show how the model bridges small-scale yielding, cohesive fracture, and brittle fracture without a priori hypotheses.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a phase-field fracture model that treats fracture as gradient-damage, where the regularization length becomes a material property. Unlike traditional approaches, this model allows arbitrary convex strength surfaces while decoupling strength, stiffness, and toughness as independent material parameters. The authors derive closed-form solutions for shear problems, propose a numerical scheme combining alternate minimization and conic programming, and verify the model's ability to bridge small-scale yielding, cohesive fracture, and brittle fracture.
AI.motivation: Traditional phase-field fracture models have a key weakness: the strength surface shape is dictated by elastic energy, and its magnitude is constrained by the regularization length. The authors aimed to develop a model where strength, stiffness, and toughness are independent material properties, allowing arbitrary strength surfaces to drive crack nucleation while enabling the model to bridge different fracture regimes without a priori hypotheses.
AI.method: The authors used the antiplane version of the phase-field model introduced in arXiv:2506.22558, which degrades strength instead of stiffness. They derived closed-form solutions for a simple shear problem, proposed a numerical scheme combining alternate minimization and conic programming, and conducted numerical simulations including a "surfing" simulation and re-entrant V-notch test.
AI.result: The model successfully verified the equivalent cohesive law, demonstrated independence from regularization when the length is small compared to the elasto-cohesive length, and showed size effect governed by the elasto-cohesive length. The re-entrant V-notch simulation confirmed the model's ability to bridge small-scale yielding, cohesive fracture, and brittle fracture without a priori hypotheses.
AI.conclusion: The proposed phase-field approach successfully unifies limit analysis, perfect plasticity, cohesive fracture, and brittle fracture into a single variational framework. By making strength, stiffness, and toughness independent material data, the model provides a more flexible and physically accurate framework for modeling fracture across different regimes.

title: Quadratic piezoelectricity from stacking-engineered interference in multilayer sliding ferroelectrics
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures; 16-page Supplementary Information included as an ancillary file
summary: Designing nonlinear piezoelectricity requires suppressing the linear piezoelectric coefficient without extinguishing higher-order electromechanical response, yet a general and reconfigurable route remains lacking. Here we introduce stacking-engineered piezoelectric interference as such a mechanism in multilayer sliding ferroelectrics. Combining first-principles calculations with a generalized Ginzburg--Landau framework, we show that each interlayer gap acts as a local piezoelectric channel whose sign and magnitude are determined by stacking. Constructive interference between same-signed channels produces a linear-dominated response, whereas destructive interference between oppositely signed channels suppresses the linear coefficient while preserving a finite quadratic response. Representative MoS$_2$ and NiTe$_2$ multilayers approach the parabolic limit, with BAAC-stacked MoS$_2$ reducing the linear-to-quadratic crossover strain by a factor of 25 relative to CBA-stacked MoS$_2$. Experimentally accessible tetralayer MoS$_2$ sliding pathways further connect linear-dominated, quadratic-dominated and sign-inverted states. Here, we identify stacking-engineered interference as a design principle for programmable nonlinear electromechanics in layered materials.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces stacking-engineered piezoelectric interference as a mechanism to design nonlinear piezoelectricity in multilayer sliding ferroelectrics. By controlling stacking order, linear piezoelectric coefficient can be suppressed while preserving higher-order electromechanical response.
AI.motivation: The challenge is to suppress the linear piezoelectric coefficient without extinguishing higher-order electromechanical response, which requires a general and reconfigurable route that currently lacks.
AI.method: First-principles calculations combined with a generalized Ginzburg-Landau framework to analyze each interlayer gap as a local piezoelectric channel.
AI.result: Constructive interference produces linear-dominated response while destructive interference suppresses linear coefficient while preserving finite quadratic response. BAAC-stacked MoS2 reduces linear-to-quadratic crossover strain by factor of 25 relative to CBA-stacked MoS2. Tetralayer MoS2 pathways connect linear-dominated, quadratic-dominated and sign-inverted states.
AI.conclusion: Stacking-engineered interference is identified as a design principle for programmable nonlinear electromechanics in layered materials.

title: Savi-Bhransha: Graph-Theoretic Dislocation-Loop Characterization in Crystals
summary: Dislocation loops govern the properties of crystalline materials, but extracting their detailed characteristics from atomistic simulations is difficult when loops are fragmented or embedded in compact defect debris. We present Savi-Bhransha, a graph-theoretic method that reconstructs interstitial and vacancy loops directly from local defect-displacement motifs, without constructing a global interface mesh. The method identifies Burgers-vector family, habit plane, loop size, segment-wise edge/screw character, and boundary and bulk defect populations for BCC, FCC, and HCP crystals. We apply it to single-cascade simulations over a range of energies in BCC W and HCP Zr, and to successive collision cascades in BCC W and FCC FeNiCr. We benchmark the method against the Dislocation Extraction Algorithm (DXA). Total dislocation lengths remain strongly correlated between the two methods, while Savi-Bhransha returns more stable loop-level objects in complex environments where DXA returns fragmented, overlapping open segments. Savi-Bhransha also better resolves mixed-morphology defects and dislocations near other defects, including vacancy clusters. Median runtime speedups are 6.34x for BCC W and 8.86x for HCP Zr, with peak-memory reductions up to 7.77x. In successive W cascades, the resolved boundary-defect concentration brackets transient-grating-spectroscopy measurements and the predicted Burgers-vector fraction agrees with room-temperature TEM. In FCC FeNiCr, the method resolves Heidenreich-Shockley dissociation, with a Shockley-pair signature in about 91% of surviving <110>-family interstitial clusters. Savi-Bhransha therefore enables efficient, topology-resolved analysis of large radiation-damage simulations and direct comparison with experimentally accessible observables.

AI.tldr: Savi-Bhransha is a graph-theoretic method for reconstructing dislocation loops from atomistic simulations in crystalline materials (BCC, FCC, HCP), offering improved loop identification, faster runtime (6-9x speedup), and better handling of complex defect environments compared to the Dislocation Extraction Algorithm (DXA).
AI.motivation: Dislocation loops are critical to crystalline material properties but are difficult to analyze when fragmented or embedded in defect debris. Existing methods like DXA struggle in complex environments, returning fragmented overlapping segments rather than stable loop-level objects.
AI.method: Graph-theoretic method that reconstructs interstitial and vacancy loops directly from local defect-displacement motifs without constructing a global interface mesh. Identifies Burgers-vector family, habit plane, loop size, segment-wise edge/screw character, and distinguishes boundary vs bulk defect populations for BCC, FCC, and HCP crystals.
AI.result: Total dislocation lengths correlate strongly with DXA. Savi-Bhransha returns more stable loop-level objects in complex environments, better resolves mixed-morphology defects and dislocations near other defects including vacancy clusters. In BCC W: 6.34x speedup, 7.77x peak-memory reduction. In HCP Zr: 8.86x speedup. In successive W cascades, resolved boundary-defect concentration brackets transient-grating-spectroscopy measurements; Burgers-vector fraction agrees with room-temperature TEM. In FCC FeNiCr, resolves Heidenreich-Shockley dissociation with Shockley-pair signature in ~91% of surviving <110>-family interstitial clusters.
AI.conclusion: Savi-Bhransha enables efficient, topology-resolved analysis of large radiation-damage simulations and direct comparison with experimentally accessible observables, making it a powerful tool for studying radiation damage in crystalline materials.

title: Resolving competing distortions in Ca0.4Sr0.6TiO3 using complementary electron and X-ray techniques
summary: We present a study of the perovskite Ca0.4Sr0.6TiO3 using variable temperature transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD). At room temperature and below, PXRD shows that the material adopts an orthorhombic Pbcm structure analogous to the P-phase of NaNbO3. Above 380 K the material transforms to a tetragonal I4/mcm phase. The structural distortions of these phases can be described as a combination of modes and order parameters associated with the M, T, $Δ$ and R-points of the Brillouin zone, each of which can be associated with a different set of superstructure reflections visible in X-ray and electron diffraction patterns. For the I4/mcm phase only the expected R-point reflections are observed in PXRD while both M and R- reflections are observed in electron diffraction. Using $Δ$ and R dark field TEM images we show that the phase transition proceeds by a loss of coherence of TiO6 octahedral tilting along the c-axis, leading to a microstructure of thin nanoscale platelets with a different local symmetry to the macroscopic structure. These persist well above the phase transition temperature and are probably responsible for the long-standing discrepancy between Raman spectroscopy and diffraction measurements in this materials system, as well as other secondary effects.

AI.tldr: The study investigates the structural phase transitions in perovskite Ca0.4Sr0.6TiO3 using variable temperature TEM and PXRD. At room temperature, the material has an orthorhombic Pbcm structure, transforming to tetragonal I4/mcm above 380 K. The transition involves loss of coherence in TiO6 octahedral tilting, creating nanoscale platelets with different local symmetry that persist above the transition temperature.
AI.motivation: This research addresses a long-standing discrepancy between Raman spectroscopy and diffraction measurements in this materials system, suggesting that nanoscale structural inhomogeneities may be responsible for the conflicting experimental observations.
AI.method: Variable temperature transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) were used to study the structural phase transitions. Structural distortions were analyzed using symmetry mode analysis associated with M, T, Δ, and R-points of the Brillouin zone. Δ and R dark field TEM imaging was employed to visualize the phase transition mechanism.
AI.result: Below 380 K, the material adopts an orthorhombic Pbcm structure (analogous to NaNbO3 P-phase). Above 380 K, it transforms to tetragonal I4/mcm phase. In the I4/mcm phase, PXRD shows only R-point reflections, while electron diffraction reveals both M and R-reflections. The transition proceeds via loss of coherence of TiO6 octahedral tilting along the c-axis, creating thin nanoscale platelets with different local symmetry that persist well above the transition temperature.
AI.conclusion: The phase transition in Ca0.4Sr0.6TiO3 occurs through a loss of coherence mechanism leading to nanoscale platelet microstructure. These persistent nanoscale domains likely explain the discrepancy between Raman spectroscopy and diffraction measurements in this materials system.

title: Layer- and Field-Dependent Magnetic Order in 2D CrSBr Revealed by Pulsed Nanocalorimetry
comment: 31 pages, 8 figures. Main text and Supplementary Information included
summary: Understanding the evolution of magnetic order in the two-dimensional limit remains a central challenge in van der Waals magnets, where thermodynamic measurements are constrained by the femtogram-scale mass of exfoliated flakes. Here, we use microsecond pulse-heating nanocalorimetry to measure the heat capacity and magnetic entropy of CrSBr flakes down to the monolayer limit. The measurements reveal the entropy landscape associated with magnetic ordering, uncovering a reduction of the interlayer transition temperature and an entropy-derived effective magnetic moment approaching the monolayer limit. Thermodynamic anomalies capture a crossover from bulk-like interlayer antiferromagnetism to a regime dominated by intralayer ferromagnetic correlations. A pronounced layer-parity effect further emerges, with odd-layer samples displaying an additional high-temperature contribution associated with uncompensated magnetic layers. Under in-plane magnetic fields applied along the easy axis, antiferromagnetic order is progressively suppressed, allowing extraction of a thickness-dependent critical field reflecting weakened interlayer exchange coupling. Entropy analysis further reveals an extended regime of magnetic fluctuations persisting well above the interlayer ordering transition. Together, these results establish nanocalorimetry as a powerful thermodynamic probe of low-dimensional magnetism, providing direct access to magnetic entropy, exchange interactions, and dimensional crossover in atomically thin van der Waals magnets.

AI.tldr: This study uses microsecond pulse-heating nanocalorimetry to investigate magnetic order evolution in CrSBr van der Waals magnets from bulk to monolayer, revealing reduced transition temperatures, layer-parity effects, and suppressed antiferromagnetism under magnetic fields.
AI.motivation: Understanding magnetic evolution in 2D van der Waals magnets is challenging due to femtogram-scale mass of exfoliated flakes limiting thermodynamic measurements. This work aims to directly measure heat capacity and magnetic entropy across thickness variations.
AI.method: Microsecond pulse-heating nanocalorimetry was employed to measure heat capacity and magnetic entropy of CrSBr flakes from bulk down to monolayer limit.
AI.result: The study found: (1) Reduced interlayer transition temperature approaching monolayer limit, (2) Entropy-derived effective magnetic moment approaching monolayer limit, (3) Crossover from interlayer antiferromagnetism to intralayer ferromagnetic correlations, (4) Layer-parity effect with odd-layers showing additional high-temperature contribution, (5) In-plane magnetic fields suppress antiferromagnetic order with thickness-dependent critical field, (6) Extended magnetic fluctuations persist above ordering transition.
AI.conclusion: Nanocalorimetry is established as a powerful thermodynamic probe for low-dimensional magnetism, providing direct access to magnetic entropy, exchange interactions, and dimensional crossover in atomically thin van der Waals magnets.

title: A versatile generalized digital twin for Electron Microscopy
summary: Development of specialized imaging and spectroscopy states in transmission electron microscopy is needed for novel applications, such as flexible momentum-resolved high energy-resolution spectroscopy. This task is complicated by the need to align and configure many different lenses, and by ambiguity as to the locations of various imaging and diffraction planes, which are often not well documented. Here we develop a versatile digital twin for simulating the electron beam trajectory throughout an electron microscope. Our code package contains simple tools for modeling the microscope column, and we present multiple procedures for dialing in precise lens locations and calibrating lens models. This enables use of the model as a predictive tool, allowing the user to quickly and easily determine the correct lens values for setting up new condenser or projector modes. Automatic procedures to change lens settings and measure the resulting changes can be used to close the loop. With the accelerating development of machine learning and artificial intelligence tools, we also believe a physically-informed model of the microscope can serve as a valuable tool for automated microscopy and AI/ML integration.

AI.tldr: A versatile digital twin simulation tool for transmission electron microscopy is developed to address challenges in aligning and configuring imaging and spectroscopy modes. The model enables predictive lens value determination and automatic calibration procedures for various condenser and projector modes.
AI.motivation: Development of specialized imaging and spectroscopy modes in TEM is needed for novel applications like flexible momentum-resolved high energy-resolution spectroscopy, but is complicated by difficulties in aligning/configuring many lenses and ambiguity in locating imaging/diffraction planes that are often poorly documented.
AI.method: Developed a versatile digital twin code package for simulating electron beam trajectory throughout an electron microscope. The package contains simple tools for modeling the microscope column, with multiple procedures for dialing in precise lens locations and calibrating lens models. Includes automatic procedures to change lens settings and measure resulting changes to close the loop.
AI.result: The model serves as a predictive tool, allowing users to quickly and easily determine correct lens values for setting up new condenser or projector modes. Automatic procedures enable closed-loop lens calibration and measurement.
AI.conclusion: A physically-informed model of the microscope can serve as a valuable tool for automated microscopy and AI/ML integration, supporting the accelerating development of machine learning and artificial intelligence tools in electron microscopy.

title: A Unified Symmetry Framework For In-plane Anomalous Hall effect
summary: The in-plane anomalous Hall effect (IPAHE), driven by an in-plane net magnetization or an applied magnetic field, challenges the conventional anomalous Hall paradigm. Despite growing interest, a unified symmetry principle governing these phenomena has remained elusive. Here, we establish a comprehensive symmetry framework that bridges the spin space group, which dictates the magnetic geometry, with the magnetic space group, which governs the anomalous Hall response. We show that spontaneous IPAHE can emerge in ferromagnets when spin-orbit-coupling-induced spin-group symmetry breaking permits additional net magnetization directions. For field-induced IPAHE, we analyze how an applied magnetic field reduces the symmetries of all 122 magnetic point groups and identify 54 groups that support IPAHE. Our framework naturally predicts IPAHE in a broad class of unconventional magnets, including altermagnets and odd-parity magnets. In particular, symmetry analysis reveals characteristic one-, two-, or three-fold angular harmonics of the Hall conductance under an in-plane rotating field, providing a symmetry-resolved fingerprint for unconventional magnetism. Using this framework, we screen the MAGNDATA database and identify candidate materials supporting spontaneous or field-induced IPAHE, encompassing ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, and unconventional magnets. Finally, we validate the symmetry predictions through first-principles calculations for two representative materials.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a unified symmetry framework connecting spin space groups (magnetic geometry) with magnetic space groups (anomalous Hall response) to explain in-plane anomalous Hall effect (IPAHE) in unconventional magnets including ferromagnets, altermagnets, and odd-parity magnets.
AI.motivation: The in-plane anomalous Hall effect challenges conventional anomalous Hall paradigms but lacks a unified symmetry principle; this work aims to fill that gap by bridging spin and magnetic space groups to explain both spontaneous and field-induced IPAHE.
AI.method: The authors developed a symmetry framework analyzing how spin-orbit-coupling-induced symmetry breaking permits additional net magnetization directions, and systematically analyzed all 122 magnetic point groups to identify 54 groups supporting field-induced IPAHE. They screened the MAGNDATA database for candidate materials and validated predictions with first-principles calculations.
AI.result: The framework predicts IPAHE in ferromagnets, altermagnets, and odd-parity magnets, revealing characteristic one-, two-, or three-fold angular harmonics of Hall conductance under in-plane rotating fields as symmetry-resolved fingerprints. Two representative materials were validated through first-principles calculations.
AI.conclusion: This symmetry-based approach provides a unified framework for understanding IPAHE in unconventional magnets and offers a practical method for screening and identifying candidate materials for experimental investigation.

title: Tuneable magnetic behaviour, electronic structure and nitrogen vacancy formation in Gd$_{x}$Sm$_{1-x}$N
comment: Copyright 2024 American Physical Society. This is the accepted manuscript of the following article: Porat, O., Joshy, E., Miller, J.D., Granville, S. and Holmes-Hewett, W.F., "Tuneable magnetic behavior, electronic structure, and nitrogen vacancy formation in Gd$_{x}$Sm$_{1-x}$N". Physical Review Materials, 8(11), p.116201, (2024). DOI: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.8.116201
summary: The rare earth nitrides are the only series of intrinsic ferromagnetic semiconductors where the interplay of spin and unquenched orbital angular momentum provides access to a range of magnetic behaviour. Furthermore, the magnetic properties can be finely tuned through the combination of multiple lanthanide ions in the nitride. Here we present a combined computational and experimental study on the electronic and magnetic properties of Gd$_x$Sm$_{1-x}$N and discuss the effect of cation substitution on the internal exchange field and band structure. We find that as the coercive field of Gd$_x$Sm$_{1-x}$N changes over orders of magnitude via cation substitution the internal exchange field changes by $\sim$20%. Control of these material properties is vital in the field of superconducting spintronics. Finally, motivated by an enhanced concentration of nitrogen vacancies in films with higher Sm content, we investigate computationally the formation of nitrogen vacancy defects in Gd$_x$Sm$_{1-x}$N finding that the formation energy is significantly reduced for vacancy sites adjacent to Sm ions rather than Gd ions.

AI.tldr: This study investigates Gd_xSm_{1-x}N, a rare earth nitride system that exhibits tunable ferromagnetic semiconductor properties through cation substitution. The research combines computational and experimental approaches to understand how replacing Gd with Sm affects magnetic properties and defect formation.
AI.motivation: The rare earth nitrides are the only intrinsic ferromagnetic semiconductors where spin and unquenched orbital angular momentum interact to produce diverse magnetic behaviors. The ability to finely tune magnetic properties through lanthanide ion combination is crucial for superconducting spintronics applications. Additionally, the observation of enhanced nitrogen vacancy concentrations in films with higher Sm content motivated investigation into vacancy formation mechanisms.
AI.method: The study employed both computational (likely DFT-based) and experimental techniques to investigate electronic and magnetic properties of Gd_xSm_{1-x}N. This included studying the effect of cation substitution on internal exchange field and band structure, as well as computational investigation of nitrogen vacancy defect formation energies at different cation sites.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) Coercive field of Gd_xSm_{1-x}N changes over orders of magnitude through cation substitution; (2) The internal exchange field changes by approximately 20% despite the large coercive field variation; (3) Nitrogen vacancy formation energy is significantly reduced at vacancy sites adjacent to Sm ions compared to Gd ions.
AI.conclusion: The magnetic properties of Gd_xSm_{1-x}N can be finely tuned through cation substitution, with dramatic changes in coercive field but more modest changes in internal exchange field. The lower nitrogen vacancy formation energy near Sm ions explains the enhanced vacancy concentration in Sm-rich films. These findings are vital for applications in superconducting spintronics where precise control of magnetic properties is essential.

title: Ordered-to-disordered transfer learning with graph neural networks for formation-energy and HOMO-LUMO gap prediction in high-entropy perovskite oxides
summary: High-entropy perovskite oxides (HEPOs) represent a chemically complex class of materials with promising functional properties, yet their vast compositional space and, chemical/structural disorder pose significant challenge for accurate property prediction. Graph neural networks (GNNs) enable rapid exploration of materials space but are often limited by the availability of representative training data. Here, we investigate ordered-to-disordered transfer learning using GNNs for formation-energy and HOMO-LUMO gap prediction in HEPOs by transferring knowledge learned from chemically ordered perovskites. Four representative GNN models, including CGCNN, GATGNN, ALIGNN and M3GNet are evaluated to understand the role of structural representations, spanning pairwise two-body and angular three-body interactions in transfer performance. We find strong property-dependent transfer behavior: formation-energy prediction transfers effectively to disordered HEPOs, whereas HOMO-LUMO gap prediction shows limited transferability due to its sensitivity to local chemical environments. Incorporating a small HEPO-specific training dataset substantially improves HOMO-LUMO gap prediction. Representation-level analysis using UMAP further highlights the importance of encoding three-body geometric information such as in ALIGNN for capturing complex structure-property relationships and improving transferability.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates transfer learning from ordered perovskites to high-entropy perovskite oxides (HEPOs) using graph neural networks (GNNs) for predicting formation energy and HOMO-LUMO gap. Four GNN models (CGCNN, GATGNN, ALIGNN, M3GNet) are evaluated, showing that formation energy transfers well but HOMO-LUMO gap requires HEPO-specific training data. ALIGNN's three-body interactions prove most effective for capturing complex structure-property relationships.
AI.motivation: The vast compositional space and chemical/structural disorder in HEPOs pose challenges for property prediction, while GNN approaches are limited by training data availability. This work aims to leverage knowledge from chemically ordered perovskites to predict properties in disordered HEPOs through transfer learning.
AI.method: Transfer learning from ordered to disordered perovskites using four GNN models (CGCNN, GATGNN, ALIGNN, M3GNet) with different structural representations (two-body and three-body interactions). UMAP is used for representation-level analysis to understand transferability.
AI.result: Formation-energy prediction transfers effectively to disordered HEPOs, while HOMO-LUMO gap prediction shows limited transferability due to sensitivity to local chemical environments. Adding small HEPO-specific training data substantially improves HOMO-LUMO gap prediction. ALIGNN's three-body geometric information proves most effective for capturing complex structure-property relationships.
AI.conclusion: Transfer learning works well for some properties (formation energy) but not others (HOMO-LUMO gap) in HEPOs. Three-body interactions in GNN representations (like ALIGNN) are crucial for transferability. Property-dependent transfer behavior should guide future transfer learning strategies in materials informatics.

title: Hidden chiral signatures in ferroaxial K2Zr(PO4)2
summary: We use first-principles calculations and multipole analyses to demonstrate the relationship between ferroaxiality and chirality in the prototypical ferroaxial material K2Zr(PO4)2. Using the atomic-site electric toroidal monopole as a measure of electronic chirality in real space, we show that, while the paraxial phase of K2Zr(PO4)2 is non-chiral, the ferroaxial phase is antiferro-chiral. By applying an electric field, we induce a ferri-chiral state with net electronic chirality which is opposite for opposite underlying ferroaxial domains and can be tuned by the direction and strength of the electric field. Associated with the real-space induced chirality, we find a distinct response in momentum space, with induced non-zero components in the Berry curvature dipole tensor that switch sign between opposite ferri-chiral domains.
